text: Here is a flat stretch of level ground, ready for launch.
This arrow shows the launch speed: twenty meters per second.
That arrow points thirty degrees above the horizontal ground.
Horizontal motion and vertical motion are completely independent of each other.
Nothing that happens vertically ever changes what happens horizontally.
The horizontal piece of that speed is seventeen point three.
The vertical piece of that same speed is exactly ten.
The setup clears away, making room for what happens next.
Three balls will now track this launch in different ways.
One is real, one tracks sideways, one tracks straight up.
All three launch together, each one going its own way.
The horizontal ball keeps a perfectly steady, unchanging speed.
But the vertical speed keeps shrinking, heading toward zero.
Right at the top, the vertical speed hits zero.
That instant lands at one second, five meters high.
Past the peak, that vertical speed reverses its direction.
It grows again, still without touching the horizontal speed.
The ball lands exactly when its vertical shadow returns down.
Total time in the air comes to two seconds.
It travels about thirty four point six meters sideways.
The ground shadow moved at one unbroken, constant pace.
The vertical shadow rose and fell on its own.
That is the independence promised at the very start.
In general, flight time equals twice vertical speed over g.
Range is simply horizontal speed multiplied by that time.
Two independent motions combined into one curved flight path.
That is projectile motion, one direction at a time.
